summary: Introductory hosted API demo focused on chat and text generation capabilities: streaming, key params (temperature, max_tokens, top_p), retries and error handling patterns. Rivergate liked streaming and retry strategies; security questions around data retention and SSO. Agreed to share pricing, benchmarks, and a pilot checklist.
topics: Request params and sampling controls (temperature, top_p)
Console walkthrough: keys, usage dashboard, logs
Optimize suggestions: batching, cache, quantization recommendations
transcript:
[00:00] Sofia Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Sofia from Redwood, and with me is Ethan from our SE team. How's everybody doing?
[00:05] Maya Thompson: Good, thanks. Excited to see the hosted API flow, we want to understand latency and cost tradeoffs.
[00:12] Carlos Reyes: Hey, quick note I'm Carlos, I'll be scope-ing the networking side.
[00:15] Ethan Park: Great, we'll pace the demo to show streaming, params, and retries—those were the main asks from your note, right Maya?
[00:22] Priya Singh: Yep, and also how the Console shows cost per route, that was important for finance.
[00:28] Sofia Patel: Perfect. Quick agenda: short intro, live demo of chat/text generation (streaming on), show key params, error/retry patterns and backoff, then Console and Optimize recommendations, Q&A, and next steps.
[00:38] Maya Thompson: Sounds good. We're on a timeline to decide by end of month, so show us what we'd need for a pilot.
[00:45] Ethan Park: Cool. I'll share my screen—bear with me while I load the sandbox.
[00:52] [screen shares - sandboxes and code snippets appear]
[01:00] Ethan Park: Ok so this is a simple curl and Node example. First call is a chat completion with streaming enabled. You can see we open an SSE stream, partial tokens come as they generate—this helps UX because you don't wait for whole doc.
[01:18] Ethan Park: (typing) I'm setting temperature 0.2, max_tokens 150, top_p 0.95. For Rivergate's use case—short financial summaries—we typically recommend low temperature to reduce hallucinations.
[01:35] Sofia Patel: Quick aside, for shorter responses and strict correctness we suggest using top_p + temperature tuned conservatively, and also use system-level prompts to constrain outputs.
[01:45] Maya Thompson: How does streaming affect cost? Do you pay per token as it streams?
[01:50] Sofia Patel: Yes, token-based billing still applies; streaming just changes when tokens are returned. There's no extra charge for streaming itself, but you can use prefix caching which reduces tokens for repeat prompts.
[02:03] Carlos Reyes: And latency? If we stream, is there overhead per chunk?
[02:07] Ethan Park: Minimal. The runtime is optimized to push tokens as they're generated. For short responses the overhead is small; it's more pronounced if you have extremely small chunk sizes.
[02:20] Priya Singh: Show the retries pattern you mentioned? We have intermittent upstream failures and want predictable client-side logic.
[02:27] Ethan Park: Sure. We recommend idempotency keys on requests for non-streaming completions; for streaming we do a resume token pattern sometimes, but easiest pattern is client-side retry with exponential backoff and a max retry count. Example here—retry after 500ms, then 1s, then 2s, cap at 5 retries. Also we surface clear 5xx vs 429 in the response so you can choose to retry or apply backoff.
[02:50] Maya Thompson: Do you recommend queuing on the client or letting the API handle spikes?
[02:55] Sofia Patel: A mix—use client-side backpressure with retries, and on our side we have autoscaling and burst capacity for hosted customers. For strict SLOs you can move to Dedicated later.
[03:10] [00:03:10] Maya Thompson: Ok that's helpful.
[03:15] Ethan Park: Now switching to params—I'll demo temperature sweep. Notice the same prompt at temp 0.0 vs 0.8; at 0.0 output is deterministic and concise, at 0.8 it's more varied. For finance summaries we usually stay 0–0.3.
[03:35] Ethan Park: Also show max_tokens—truncate or allow stream to end; if you set stop tokens it helps avoid trailing boilerplate.
[03:46] Carlos Reyes: We use stop tokens to redact if there are PII patterns—does Redwood provide content filtering or PII redaction?
[03:53] Sofia Patel: We provide optional content filters and you can run a PII detection pipeline. For Private deployments you can route those through a customer-managed pipeline.
[04:04] Priya Singh: On the Console, can you show where we see cost per route and model?
[04:09] Ethan Park: Switch to Console view—here's per-route token breakdown, latencies, and cost buckets. You can drill down to API key or route and see sample traces.
[04:25] [screen shows console with graphs]
[04:29] Maya Thompson: Nice, that sample trace is useful—does it show prompt+response token counts?
[04:33] Ethan Park: Yes, and token-level latency. We also tag requests with model and region so you can filter by those.
[04:42] Maya Thompson: Can you set alerting on spikes or regressions?
[04:45] Sofia Patel: Yup, pre-built alerts for token cost, error rate, and latency, and custom threshold alerts. Also Quality monitoring—you can tie eval prompt sets to detect regressions in generation quality.
[04:58] Maya Thompson: Good. Security: a few questions—where are logs stored, what's retention, and do you have SOC2?
[05:05] Sofia Patel: We are SOC2 Type II; logs are stored in our control plane with configurable retention. For Hosted, default retention is 90 days but you can request longer retention as an add-on or use Private where logs stay in your VPC. We support SAML SSO, RBAC, and KMS integration for key wrapping.
[05:25] Carlos Reyes: For compliance we need audit logs and an option to disable prompt storage—can you do that?
[05:31] Ethan Park: Yes, you can opt out of storing prompts or enable redaction. For the hosted product we have data retention controls and an enterprise add-on for stricter controls.
[05:42] Maya Thompson: What about throughput? If we have bursty end-of-month loads, how do you handle queueing?
[05:48] Sofia Patel: Hosted supports autoscaling and burst pools; you can also buy reserved Dedicated capacity for guaranteed throughput. Optimize can recommend batching and quantization profiles to reduce cost while preserving latency.
[06:00] Priya Singh: Can you explain batching tradeoffs? We're worried about latency increases.
[06:05] Ethan Park: Sure—continuous batching groups concurrent requests to improve GPU utilization. For latency-sensitive short requests, we keep max_batch_ms small to avoid tail latency. For less latency-sensitive workloads, larger batch windows reduce cost. Optimize will analyze your traffic and recommend batching configs.
[06:22] Maya Thompson: Are there any quick wins for us? Small change we can do immediately?
[06:26] Ethan Park: Prefix caching for repeated prompts and lowering temperature to reduce token length help. Also set sensible max_tokens and use stop sequences. We'll include an Optimize report in the pilot.
[06:36] Carlos Reyes: Networking—what IPs to allowlist?
[06:39] Sofia Patel: We'll send a short allowlist doc with our endpoint ranges; if you need fixed egress IPs we can discuss dedicated peering or a static egress add-on.
[06:50] Maya Thompson: Ok. For pilot success criteria, we'd need under 500ms 95th percentile for our 150-token summaries, and cost under $X per 1k requests—can you help validate?
[07:02] Sofia Patel: Absolutely—Ethan will run a quick benchmark with your sample prompts once you provide them, and we'll tune model choice and batching.
[07:10] Priya Singh: Do you have recommended models for finance summarization?
[07:14] Ethan Park: We include curated open models and Redwood-verified profiles. For higher fidelity we suggest the 'redwood-medium-01' variant (not exact naming in notes) or a larger variant if you need more context. We'll pick based on your latency/cost targets.
[07:29] Maya Thompson: Any vendor lock-in concerns if we start hosted and later move to Dedicated or Private?
[07:34] Sofia Patel: We design the API to be consistent across hosted, dedicated, and private. Rollouts and model pins are portable, so switching deployment mode is mainly infra and contract changes, not a rewrite.
[07:45] [07:45] Ethan Park: Quick demo of error codes—here's a 429 for rate limit, we expose headers for retry-after, and we return structured error bodies so you can distinguish quota vs server errors.
[07:58] Priya Singh: How do you recommend client retry logic for 429s vs 5xx?
[08:02] Ethan Park: For 429s use the retry-after header and exponential backoff; for 5xx apply a slightly longer backoff and fewer retries. Use idempotency keys for non-streaming flows.
[08:15] Maya Thompson: Ok good. Anything about model drift detection?
[08:19] Sofia Patel: Quality monitoring ties to eval sets—you can run a baseline and then alerts notify if responses diverge. We also support automated A/B rollouts with canary percentages.
[08:30] Carlos Reyes: Onboarding timeline—how quickly can we run a pilot?
[08:33] Sofia Patel: If we have sample traffic this week, we can spin up a pilot within 5 business days. We'll need IP allowlist and an account to issue keys.
[08:45] Maya Thompson: Great.
[08:48] Priya Singh: Any gotchas we should watch for?
[08:51] Ethan Park: Watch prompt tokenization—some punctuation increases token count unexpectedly; run a tokenization pass on your prompts. Also truncation behavior if context windows exceed model limits.
[09:03] Sofia Patel: Quick recap and next steps: we'll share pricing + region availability, Ethan will send a benchmark checklist and a small harness, Maya to share prompt list and sample traffic, Carlos to confirm network allowlisting. Schedule pilot kickoff week of 5/18.
[09:20] Maya Thompson: Sounds good to me. Thanks all.
[09:23] Carlos Reyes: Thanks.
[09:25] Sofia Patel: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up by email with the docs and next steps.
[09:30] [call ends]
